shared.title: Grade 6 Discovery Rotations
shared.bigQuestion: What can we learn about ourselves and a stronger Grade 6 community while protecting each person's choices and privacy?
shared.summary: The opening schedule may change by group, day, and block length. For each visit, the teacher chooses one complete paper-first organizer: Identity Constellation, How I Learn Best, Ideal Learning Space, Build a Better Grade 6, or Grade 6 Quest Map. On that selected page, students visit every labelled region, deepen safe choices, add accessible visual meaning-making across the whole organizer, decide what remains private, and submit named originals face-down for private transfer. Blank/skip needs no explanation, and accommodation may reduce substantive output without creating catch-up work. No student must complete all five, visit in sequence, use AI, or post this work to SpacesEDU.

learningArc.label: Identity Constellation
learningArc.studentAction: Represent chosen people, places, interests, languages, strengths, or experiences with words, symbols, pictures, and connections.
learningArc.outcome: Students make identity and privacy choices without required personal disclosure.

learningArc.label: How I Learn Best
learningArc.studentAction: Name useful learning conditions, one way to recover when stuck, a strength, and a support to try.
learningArc.outcome: The receiving teacher gains practical learner information without fixed learning-style labels.

learningArc.label: Ideal Learning Space
learningArc.studentAction: Design and label a space for focus, collaboration, access, movement, and reset.
learningArc.outcome: Students reason about inclusive design, constraints, and trade-offs.

learningArc.label: Build a Better Grade 6
learningArc.studentAction: Propose a small improvement, name who it helps, test a trade-off, and identify the right decision-maker.
learningArc.outcome: Student voice is connected to evidence, democratic process, feasibility, and accountability.

learningArc.label: Grade 6 Quest Map
learningArc.studentAction: Map a meaningful goal to a challenge, strengths, help sources, and a first step.
learningArc.outcome: Students practise hopeful, realistic planning and help-seeking without turning goals into contracts.

thinkingMoves.prompt: Who is helped, who could be excluded, and what constraint or authority matters?

thinkingMoves.prompt: Whose experience or need is missing, and how can we ask without demanding disclosure?

teacher.timing: Opening rotations · schedule, order, and end date still flexible
teacher.duration: Choose a complete 45-, 60-, or 75-minute route after the group and block are known
teacher.grouping: Whole-class provocation and modelling; independent organizer creation with optional partner or teacher check. Every session stands alone, and students may not complete every organizer or visit in the same order.
teacher.launch: Choose the session by purpose, time, and what this group has already completed. Before content, state what is private, what may become a separately copied display excerpt, and that blanks or fictional routes are valid.
prepare: Open Opening Rotations and choose one organizer plus the 45-, 60-, or 75-minute route only after the arriving group and block are known.
Keep the verified five-page Discovery Booklet available digitally; wait for the confirmed schedule before printing class sets.
Gather pencils, optional colour supplies, and one labelled opaque folder or envelope for each room/date/rotation block.

Prepare one concise, safe whole-page model that visits every labelled region through a response choice, including fictional, blank/skip, and privacy-marker routes; never model with confidential student information.
Confirm who will privately sort named originals by final roster and transfer them to receiving teachers.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Name the learning intention, disclosure choices, and display boundary before students begin.
Use the selected organizer's opening image, scenario, or comparison; ask one question and protect quiet think time.
Briefly visit every region in a safe model using several equivalent response modes, including fictional, blank/skip, and privacy-marker choices.
Students visit every labelled region, deepen safe choices, and add one or more accessible visual cues across the page. Confer without pressuring disclosure or grading artistry.
Use a quiet gallery, partner conference, or teacher check; the 75-minute route adds the organizer-specific deepening.
Students use success indicators, revise one part, and decide what remains private.
Students label the back and submit named originals face-down into the correct opaque folder.

lookFors: Makes a response choice in every labelled region; a fictional alternative, blank/skip, or privacy marker counts without explanation, and accommodation may reduce substantive output.
Uses accessible visual meaning-making across the whole page; colour and artistic polish are never required or assessed.
Connects a design, proposal, preference, or goal to a reason, person, condition, or next step.
Notices a trade-off, missing perspective, access need, or useful support when the selected organizer calls for it.
Revises one part after a self, peer, or teacher check.
Makes and communicates a privacy choice without being judged on the amount disclosed.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Treat every organizer as formative only. Students label the back with name, organizer, room/date or rotation block, WHOLE PAGE COMPLETE—including privacy-safe blank/skip or accommodation—or PAUSED—ASK BEFORE OFFERING MORE TIME, plus the privacy/display choice. Collect named originals face-down in an opaque folder, sort once by final roster, and pass them privately to receiving teachers. Do not grade, rank, diagnose, use for placement, require catch-up for an accommodation, or post named originals to SpacesEDU. Display only a separately copied, student-selected excerpt or approved design after asking again.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Grade 6 Discovery Rotations
student.why: Each organizer gives you a different way to show what matters to you, what helps learning, what could improve Grade 6, or what path you want to begin. You decide what is safe to share.
student.summary: Your group will complete and decorate one whole, standalone Discovery organizer. Visit every labelled region on today's page using words, symbols, pictures, dictation, a model, a fictional alternative, blank/skip, or a privacy marker. A skip needs no explanation, accommodation can change how much you produce, and artistic polish is not graded. You do not need to complete every page or share private information.
student.grouping: Whole-class opening, individual creation, and an optional partner or teacher check
bring: A pencil or another way to create
Your choices, ideas, and willingness to revise
No private story, diagnosis, family detail, or public sharing is required
student.firstMove: Listen for today's organizer question, then make a quick response choice in every labelled region before returning to deepen safe ideas and add visual meaning across the page.

quickReference.firstMove: Quick-pass every labelled region with a safe response, fictional alternative, blank/skip, or privacy marker; no reason is needed for a skip.
quickReference.handIn: Label the back and put the named original face-down in the rotation folder. It is practice, not a grade.
quickReference.missed: Ask which organizer your group completed. Every page is standalone, so no earlier session is required.

student.firstMoveNote: You may mark blank/skip without explaining why, use a fictional route, or ask for a scribe, word bank, or reduced-output accommodation. Those choices still complete the region and do not create catch-up work.
steps: Choose: hear the question, privacy boundary, and several ways to respond.
First pass: make a response choice in every labelled region, including blank/skip when useful.
Deepen + decorate: develop safe choices and use drawing, symbols, borders, spacing, patterns, or colour to carry meaning across the whole page.
Check: use the success clues with yourself, a partner, or the teacher.
Revise: improve one part and decide what remains private.
Label and submit: place the named original face-down in the correct folder.
choices: Use words, symbols, pictures, labelled drawings, dictation to an adult, speech-to-text on an approved shared device, or a simple model.
Use a fictional or school-safe example, replace a prompt, choose quiet work, or leave a private area blank.
Choose whether one safe idea may be copied later; the named original stays private unless a teacher asks again.
student.product: One complete, decorated Discovery organizer with every labelled region visited through a response choice, a student-chosen level of disclosure, and one visible revision or next step when useful.
student.finish: Every labelled region has a response choice—including blank/skip when useful—visual cues help the whole page make sense, and you can explain one safe idea or revision plus what remains private. Artistry is not assessed.
student.handInOrSave: Label the back and submit the named original face-down. It travels privately to your receiving teacher and is not graded or used for placement.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Every organizer starts fresh. Ask for the whole-page shortened route, a model, word bank, scribe, fictional example, blank/skip, or a reduced-output accommodation that does not create catch-up work.
student.spacesNote: Discovery organizers are not posted to SpacesEDU. Later, you may choose a safe idea as part of a separate Learning Story.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: Grade 6 Discovery Rotations
family.summary: During the opening rotations, each group completes one of five standalone paper organizers. Sessions explore identity, learning conditions, inclusive spaces, ideas for a better Grade 6, or a meaningful goal. The visit order and length may differ by group, and students are not expected to complete every organizer.
family.whyThisMatters: Several low-stakes routes help teachers notice student voice, strengths, reasoning, access needs, hopes, and community ideas without asking children to reveal private information or perform for a public display.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students visit every labelled region on one selected organizer using words, symbols, pictures, dictation, design, a fictional alternative, blank/skip, or another accessible route; add visual meaning across the whole page; use a simple success check; revise when useful; choose what stays private; and submit the named original face-down for private teacher transfer.

quickReference.atSchool: Each group completes one standalone Discovery organizer with an opening question, creation time, a check, revision, and private handoff.
quickReference.home: Nothing to prepare or finish at home.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher observes agency, representation, reasoning, and revision. The organizer is practice—not a grade, diagnosis, or placement decision.
quickReference.spaces: Named originals stay with the teacher and are not posted. A student may later choose a safe idea for a separate Learning Story.

family.product: One complete, decorated Discovery organizer selected for the group and available block; no-explanation blank/skip and accommodation routes remain valid completion choices.
family.assessment: This is low-stakes formative evidence. Teachers notice agency, reasoning, representation, access choices, and revision. The page is not graded, ranked, diagnosed, or used for class placement.
family.agreementNote: Students choose what to disclose. Diagnoses, family details, difficult experiences, public sharing, and personal goals are never required. Blank/skip needs no explanation, a fictional route can be thoughtful, accommodation may reduce substantive output without catch-up, and artistic polish is not assessed.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Whole-class questions and optional partner checks support community thinking. Named originals travel privately to receiving teachers; only a separate student-approved copy or excerpt may be considered for display.

shared.title: Five ways to become known
shared.bigQuestion: What can we learn about ourselves, one another, and this place without asking anyone to share a private story?
shared.summary: Across five connected days, students tell a low-risk object story, show how they reason with number size, name useful learning conditions, gather exact observations from the school grounds, and choose one specific example for a Friday Learning Story. If opening rotations are still finishing for some groups, use the standalone organizer route without treating it as missed prerequisite work.

learningArc.label: Story
learningArc.studentAction: Choose an ordinary object, point to five visible clues, tell a three-beat story, and improve it after one listener question.
learningArc.outcome: The class begins with voice, listening, visible evidence, and a safe fictional route.

learningArc.label: Number
learningArc.studentAction: Place very large and very small quantities on accurate scales and explain one surprising position.
learningArc.outcome: The teacher sees strategies and misconceptions without reducing students to a score.

learningArc.label: Learning
learningArc.studentAction: Test which conditions help in real classroom situations and write one useful request or strategy.
learningArc.outcome: Students describe changeable supports and actions rather than fixed learning labels.

learningArc.label: Place
learningArc.studentAction: Collect exact sound, movement, colour, light, and texture evidence outside or from an equivalent observation station.
learningArc.outcome: Observation stays separate from inference, and the class gathers material for a place response.

learningArc.label: Synthesize
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one specific example, name what it shows, set one realistic goal, and revise for a teacher or family audience.
learningArc.outcome: One meaningful Learning Story replaces several small uploads.

teacher.launch: This week gives us five different ways to notice how people think and learn. Nobody has to share a private or painful story. We will use specific evidence, listen carefully, and revise one idea each day.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Model one low-stakes three-beat story, then protect partner telling, listener questions, and one clear retell.
Use the projected number scale, require predictions before reveals, and record strategies rather than ranking students.
Use classroom cases, avoid fixed labels, and have students name one support or action they can explain.
Teach observation versus inference, follow the safe route, and offer an equivalent stationary or indoor route.
Students choose one strong example, add a realistic goal and first step, revise for an audience, and make the single September post.

lookFors: Points to exact story, number, or place evidence before making an inference.
Listens closely enough to ask a useful question or restate a partner's idea accurately.
Explains a strategy, support, contribution, or revision with a specific example.

teacher.evidenceHandoff: Use conversation, notebooks, quick models, observation, and conferences as formative evidence. student.routeTitle: Five ways to show your learning

Name: identify a learning condition or action that helps in a real situation.
Notice: collect exact evidence from the school grounds or an equivalent observation station.

family.summary: Students are introduced through several kinds of classroom evidence: oral story and listening, number reasoning, learning conditions, exact place observations, collaboration, and reflection. No student is required to share a private or painful story.
family.whyThisMatters: One task cannot show the whole learner. The week gives the teacher multiple low-stakes ways to notice strengths, strategies, participation, supports, and questions before students choose one example for a Friday Learning Story.
family.whatStudentsDo: Monday begins with ordinary-object storytelling. Tuesday uses a visual number investigation. Wednesday names changeable learning conditions and supports. Thursday gathers place observations. Friday students synthesize one meaningful example and a realistic first goal.

quickReference.atSchool: Students tell, estimate, discuss, observe, create, and revise across five connected days.
quickReference.home: Nothing to finish or prepare at home. A short conversation about one specific example is welcome.

quickReference.spaces: One Friday Learning Story is posted; the week's practice remains in class.

family.product: One student-selected Friday Learning Story with evidence of a strength or contribution, useful learning conditions, and one realistic goal.
family.assessment: Early formative evidence only. The teacher looks for specific examples, explanation, listening, strategy, revision, and a feasible next step.
family.agreementNote: Students may use fictional, observation-only, written, spoken, visual, or recorded routes. Private family, medical, diagnostic, or painful information is not required.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Pairs and groups create several opportunities to hear student thinking. The final Learning Story is individual so each learner chooses the evidence and goal that genuinely fit.

shared.title: Who decides—and what does this place teach us?
shared.bigQuestion: How can maps, sources, local voices, and public decisions change what we understand about Surrey?
shared.summary: Students use the existing place, map, evidence, perspective, and government lessons as a live Surrey case. They distinguish observation from inference, learn from attributed local-Nation and district sources, sort who controls which decisions, and begin checking election claims after the official candidate list is available.

learningArc.label: Who decides?
learningArc.studentAction: Sort school, district, city, provincial, and federal decisions; explain the exact authority involved.
learningArc.outcome: Students distinguish influence, administration, voting, oversight, and final authority.

learningArc.label: Learn with place
learningArc.studentAction: Gather local observations and compare what different maps and attributed sources make visible or leave out.
learningArc.outcome: Place learning remains specific to source, Nation, speaker, purpose, and protocol.

learningArc.label: Check a campaign claim
learningArc.studentAction: Label fact, opinion, claim, or promise; trace one checkable part to an official or independent source.
learningArc.outcome: A campaign statement becomes evidence to investigate, not a position students are told to support.

learningArc.label: Make meaning
learningArc.studentAction: Build a concise place-and-decision display with exact source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one next question.
learningArc.outcome: The display makes local learning visible without turning a generic craft into reconciliation.

learningArc.label: Carry it forward
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one election, place, or power question worth following in the October Newsroom.
learningArc.outcome: Strong questions continue; no extra SpacesEDU post is required.

teacher.timing: Surrey, place, and election inquiry · Sept. 21–30

teacher.grouping: Whole-class source launches; pairs for close reading and claim checks; groups of 3–4 for jurisdiction sorting and display design; individual reflection only when each student's own question matters.
teacher.launch: We are going to look closely at decisions and sources connected to the place outside our classroom. Our job is not to choose a candidate. It is to work out who can decide, what the evidence supports, whose perspective is present, and what still needs checking.
prepare: Open the existing Social Studies lessons Three Maps of Fleetwood, Power Is Already in the Room or Same Crisis, Different Systems, Perspective Without Guessing, and Trace the Claim.
Use the Surrey election bridge and official source doors. After Sept. 11, use the official candidate information rather than provisional lists.

Prepare a no-Wi-Fi route: source title and credit on the board, one short permitted excerpt or teacher notes, a projected or printed map, and notebooks.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Sort exact school, trustee, city, provincial, and federal scenarios; require the decision and authority, not only the topic.
Compare what a street map, planning map, and First Peoples' map make visible; keep source, purpose, and limits attached.
Return to local observation, then learn directly from one attributed local or district-curated source without turning it into a generic Indigenous claim.
Use stated evidence to identify who is affected and whose perspective is still missing; do not ask students to invent community voices.
Compare one dated campaign statement with the original official data, policy, budget, or jurisdiction source. Report supported, contradicted, or uncertain.
Groups build a concise display with source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one question. Use the Newsroom to choose what deserves following in October.

Can explain how people who are not old enough to vote may still participate responsibly.

Explain: state what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain.
choices: Investigate through a map, image, short text, audio, or a teacher-read excerpt from the same credited source.
Compare a claim or missing perspective without endorsing or opposing a candidate.
Contribute by pointing, sorting, speaking, writing, or drawing; your teacher can provide a shared-screen or paper route.
student.product: A concise group display with exact source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one question worth following.
student.finish: You can identify who has authority for a decision, use a dated source as evidence, name a missing perspective without inventing it, and keep one uncertainty visible.
student.handInOrSave: Keep the display and source trail in class. Your teacher will say if one later reflection belongs in an existing portfolio pathway.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Begin with one visible clue and the source credit. Ask: Who made this? When? What exact decision or claim is involved?

family.assessment: Formative assessment focuses on evidence, authority, source care, reasoning, uncertainty, and respectful discussion. Candidate preference is never assessed.

shared.title: Before the vote: claims, responsibilities, and choices
shared.bigQuestion: How can we compare election choices without confusing a persuasive promise with evidence that it can happen?
shared.summary: Students continue the existing Surrey election case through Trace the Claim, the Newsroom, and Civic Decision Brief. They compare directly sourced statements about the same issue, check what mayor, council, and trustees can actually decide, weigh trade-offs, and prepare for the existing Student Vote process without adding another unit or portfolio post.

learningArc.label: Match power
learningArc.studentAction: Match candidate statements to the office's real responsibilities and flag anything that needs council, the Board of Education, the province, funding, or time.
learningArc.outcome: Students distinguish leadership and influence from decisions one winner can make alone.

learningArc.label: Trace a claim
learningArc.studentAction: Use Trace the Claim and a dated source trail to label fact, opinion, claim, or promise and verify one checkable part.
learningArc.outcome: Students report supported, contradicted, or still uncertain instead of reacting to confidence or style.

learningArc.label: Compare fairly
learningArc.studentAction: Place directly sourced statements about one issue on a common comparison board: proposal, evidence, authority, trade-off, missing perspective, and question.
learningArc.outcome: Candidates are compared by the same inquiry criteria without a teacher ranking or endorsement.

learningArc.label: Hear and question
learningArc.studentAction: Use the existing Civic Decision Brief hearing to present evidence, ask neutral follow-up questions, and revise one conclusion.
learningArc.outcome: Public reasoning stays separate from anyone's private ballot choice.

learningArc.label: Student Vote
learningArc.studentAction: Learn the ballot routine, serve in election-worker roles, and vote privately through the existing Student Vote structure when the class is registered.
learningArc.outcome: Students practise an election process after learning the offices, evidence, and responsibilities.

visual.alt: Grade 6 students using common evidence cards in a classroom civic hearing while classmates listen and prepare questions.
visual.caption: Use the same evidence questions for every candidate: What is proposed? Who has authority? What supports it? What is the trade-off?

thinkingMoves.label: Verify

thinkingMoves.label: Challenge assumptions
thinkingMoves.prompt: Are we assuming one person can decide what requires a council, board, budget, approval, or time?

thinkingMoves.label: Shift perspective
thinkingMoves.prompt: Who is affected, who is speaking, and whose view is still missing?

thinkingMoves.label: Weigh trade-offs
thinkingMoves.prompt: Who may benefit, what may it cost, and what could be given up?

thinkingMoves.label: Reflect
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which evidence changed or complicated our thinking?

prepare: Open the official City of Surrey candidate list and role descriptions through the existing Surrey election source doors; use directly sourced candidate material, not search snippets or unsourced comparison pages.

Choose one age-appropriate issue and short statements that can be compared with the same criteria. Include the date, speaker, office sought, original link, and enough context to avoid changing the meaning.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Check the promise before the vote
student.why: Candidates use facts, opinions, claims, and promises to persuade voters. You can check the source, the office's real power, and the trade-offs before making up your own mind.
student.summary: Work with a partner and team to trace one claim, compare statements with the same questions, take part in a civic hearing, and prepare for a private Student Vote ballot.
student.grouping: Pairs and teams for investigation; whole class for the hearing; a private individual ballot
bring: One source detail you can point to
A question that does not assume the answer
Respect for other people's private choices
student.firstMove: Read one short campaign statement. Underline the exact promise. Circle what could be checked. Put a question mark beside anything the office may not control alone.
student.firstMoveNote: A strong promise can still require a council or board vote, money, another level of government, public input, or time.

quickReference.firstMove: Underline the promise, circle the checkable part, and question the office's authority.
quickReference.handIn: Keep the pair claim trail and team comparison board in class. Your ballot choice stays private.
quickReference.missed: Open one dated statement and its original source. Add the office, one checkable claim, and one honest uncertainty.

steps: Identify: Who said it, when, and which office are they seeking?
Label: Is it a fact, opinion, claim, or promise?
Trace: Open the original source for the strongest checkable part.
Match: Can this office decide it alone, act with others, influence it, or not control it?
Compare: Use the same headings for every candidate statement.
Question: Ask about evidence, cost, trade-offs, missing perspectives, or what happens next.
Decide privately: Use the Student Vote ballot only after you understand the offices and evidence.
choices: Use a teacher-read excerpt, projected source, short text, audio, or paper source card with the same credit and context.
Contribute by pointing, sorting, speaking, writing, drawing a decision path, or asking a question.
Change your mind, remain uncertain, or keep your ballot choice private; your political preference is not assessed.
student.product: One pair claim trail, one team comparison board, and a short reflection on the evidence or process—not on which name you chose.
student.finish: You can check a campaign statement, explain what the office can and cannot do alone, compare choices fairly, and protect ballot privacy.
student.handInOrSave: Keep investigation notes and the comparison board in class. Follow the class Student Vote routine; never put your ballot choice in SpacesEDU.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Start with one statement and four questions: Who said it? What is promised? What evidence checks it? Who has the power to act?
student.spacesNote: No extra SpacesEDU post is planned. Your ballot choice remains private.

shared.eyebrow: OCTOBER · RESULTS AND WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
shared.title: Election day to next steps: what happens now?
shared.bigQuestion: What do election results tell us—and what still has to happen before a promise becomes a public decision?
shared.summary: Students use the Newsroom to read official Surrey results and CIVIX Student Vote results when each is released. They compare patterns carefully, follow one promise through the people, votes, budgets, approvals, and time it may require, and identify ways people can continue to influence public decisions after election day.

learningArc.label: Election day
learningArc.studentAction: Notice which Surrey offices are being elected and wait for official, dated results rather than reposting early claims or guesses.
learningArc.outcome: Students understand that result status and source matter.

learningArc.label: Read the results
learningArc.studentAction: Open the official Surrey results and record office, names, totals or shares, result status, source, and update time.
learningArc.outcome: The class builds an accurate result record for mayor, council, and school trustees.

learningArc.label: Compare carefully
learningArc.studentAction: Compare official and Student Vote results when both are available; describe a pattern without guessing why it happened.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate numerical patterns from unsupported explanations about voters.

learningArc.label: Follow a promise
learningArc.studentAction: Trace one promise through the council or board decision, staff work, budget, other approvals, public input, and time it may require.
learningArc.outcome: Winning an election is distinguished from having unlimited or immediate power.

learningArc.label: Keep participating
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one respectful next action a young person could take: follow a meeting, ask a question, write, verify, speak, create, volunteer, or revisit the evidence.
learningArc.outcome: Democratic participation continues between elections.

visual.caption: Record the source and result status first. Then describe the pattern, test explanations, and follow one promise into the real decision process.

teacher.launch: An election chooses people for public roles. Does winning mean they can now do everything they promised? What evidence would show the difference between being elected and making a decision happen?

runOfShow.teacherAction: Project the official source. Record what is known, the result status and update time, and one question. Do not fill gaps from social posts or memory.
Pairs describe one official/Student Vote similarity or difference when both are available. Separate what the numbers show from hypotheses about why.
Teams move one pre-election promise through the real pathway. Require the collective body, budget or approval, staff role, time, and review point that apply.
Students name a respectful way to keep following or influencing a public decision. Close with one question for a future Newsroom check rather than a new assignment.

lookFors: Records the official source, update time, and whether a result is preliminary or final.
Describes a numerical pattern without claiming it proves voters' motives.

Returns to a pre-election promise and identifies a realistic next decision or accountability point.
Names a specific, respectful way young people can continue participating.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Results are the beginning, not the end
student.why: Election results tell us who was chosen. They do not prove why everyone voted, and they do not give one winner unlimited power.
student.summary: Read official Surrey results, compare them with Student Vote results when available, follow one promise through the real decision path, and choose a way young people can keep participating.
student.grouping: Whole class, pairs, and teams; one short personal next-step reflection
bring: The source name and update time
One pattern the numbers actually show
One question about what happens next
student.firstMove: Find the result source, its update time, and its status. Write one sentence that begins, ‘This result shows…’ and one that begins, ‘This result does not show…’
student.firstMoveNote: Wait for official results. A total or percentage shows a pattern; it does not automatically explain people's reasons.

quickReference.firstMove: Record source, update time, and status. Say what the result shows and does not show.
quickReference.handIn: Keep the result note and promise pathway in class. No extra SpacesEDU post is planned.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the official result source and one promise. Add one accurate pattern and one next step the promise would require.

steps: Verify: use the official Surrey result and record when it was updated.

Compare: add Student Vote results when released and name one similarity or difference.
Trace: follow one promise through the people, collective vote, money, approvals, public input, and time it needs.
Question: identify what should be checked at a future council or Board meeting.
Continue: choose one respectful way a young person can follow or influence the issue.
choices: Read a projected chart, paper result table, teacher-read numbers, audio description, or the original result page.
Show a comparison by speaking, writing, pointing, arranging cards, or drawing the promise pathway.
Keep your ballot choice private and discuss results without guessing how classmates or families voted.

student.finish: You can say what the results show and do not show, explain why winners still share power, and name a way participation continues.

family.whatStudentsDo: Students verify the result source and status, compare official and Student Vote patterns without guessing at voters' motives, follow one earlier promise through a decision pathway, and identify ways participation continues after election day.
